spec.title: Offered vs handled rate (req/s)
spec.description: Offered = k6 iterations + dropped (what k6 tried to send). Handled = 202 answers counted by the server. Where handled stays under offered, the system is the limit. Expect about 2150 offered in every run. Prediction: pool 5 handles about 925, pool 10 about 1850, pool 25 and up about 2150. Surprising: handled above offered (a stale series from an earlier run, check testid), or pool 90 handling much less than pool 25.

spec.title: Latency seen by k6: p50 / p99
spec.description: k6 native histogram (no _bucket series). Healthy pool: p50 a few ms. Prediction for pool 10: p50 about 1.6 s (3000 VUs / 1865 req/s), like B1. Surprising: low latency together with many errors (fast 503 at pool 120 can look like good latency, read this with the error panel). k6 series are not marked stale after a run, the last value can linger for minutes.

spec.title: k6 p99 by pool size (pool_max tag)
spec.description: One curve per pool size, from the k6 tag pool_max. This is the p99-vs-pool-size picture for the report: expected to improve from 5 to 25 and then flatten. Repeats of the same size appear as separate time segments (run order is 5..120, 120..5, 5..120).

spec.title: Errors per second by type (server)
spec.description: ep_db_errors_by_type_total split by cause: pool_timeout (waited over 2 s for a connection), too_many_clients (Postgres refused: max_connections), statement_timeout, other. Prediction: pool_timeout at pool 5 (only if capacity < 1500 req/s), too_many_clients at pool 120, nothing in between. This metric is NOT in the inventory until the first error of a type happens (see missing-metrics.txt): No data is normal for a healthy run. Surprising: type other.

spec.title: Responses by status (server)
spec.description: 202 turning into 503 is the failure. Only 202 and 503 are expected. A 500 means something unhandled: read server.out of that run.

spec.title: Pool state vs configured max
spec.description: ep_pg_pool_total = open connections, idle = free, waiting = requests queued, max = PG_POOL_MAX. Pool 5 and 10: total = max and waiting high. Pool 25 and up: waiting about 0. Pool 120: total should stop near the usable slots (about 95), never reach 120. Surprising: total below max while waiting > 0 (the pool is still opening connections, or connecting fails).

spec.title: Pool wait vs query time (p50 / p99)
spec.description: Pool wait = time queued in Node before getting a connection. Query time = INSERT on an acquired connection, includes the commit (fsync). Wait much larger than query time: the pool is the bottleneck. Both large: Postgres or the disk. Prediction: wait dominates at pool 5 and 10; query time grows at pool 50 to 90 if connections hurt. The top histogram bucket is 2.5 s: larger values are clamped.

spec.title: In-flight requests vs Little's Law
spec.description: In-flight = requests inside the server now. Little's Law: in-flight = rate x mean time, and rate(duration_sum) is exactly that average, so the two lines should match. Growth is the queue. At pool 10 it should grow until about the VU cap of 3000.

spec.title: Postgres connections by state
spec.description: pg_stat_activity_count from postgres-exporter, summed by state (active = running a query, idle = connected and waiting), with max_connections and usable slots (max minus superuser_reserved_connections) as reference lines. Prediction: the total follows the pool size up to about 95 and then stays flat even at pool 120. CAVEAT: I have only seen the HELP line of pg_stat_activity_count, not its labels; I assume a `state` label. If the legend shows a single series, check the labels in Explore. The exporter and my psql checks count as connections too.

spec.title: Pool-bound ceiling: pool max / mean query time vs handled
spec.description: Ceiling = PG_POOL_MAX / mean time a connection is held (query duration includes the commit). Handled should stay under the ceiling and hug it when the pool is the limit (pool 5 and 10). At pool 25 and up the ceiling is far above 2150: the pool is not the limit any more. Surprising: handled above the ceiling (hold time measured wrongly).

spec.title: Postgres commits/s vs disk writes/s
spec.description: Commits per second (all databases, postgres-exporter) next to disk write operations per second (node_exporter, whole host). Group commit: commits/s well above disk writes/s means many commits share one flush; more connections should raise the ratio. Surprising: equal values at pool 25 or more.

spec.title: Postgres container CPU (cores)
spec.description: CPU of the whole Postgres container (user and system), limit 2 cores (cpus: 2). Prediction: rises with pool size, more system time at 50 to 90. Near 2.0 means CPU-bound; throttled seconds above 0 mean the cpus: 2 limit is biting. Comes from pg-container-exporter.sh (job node, needs cgroup v2, else No data).

spec.title: Postgres container memory
spec.description: cgroup memory.current of the container: includes page cache and shared_buffers, not only backend memory. Prediction: about +200 to +400 MB at pool 50 and +350 to +700 MB at pool 90 (limit 2 GiB). It grows in the first seconds of each run as backends appear. Surprising: flat memory at pool 90 (connections not really opened).

spec.title: Container memory per Postgres connection (rough)
spec.description: Container memory divided by all connections (all states, including exporter and psql). Rough trend only, not the real size of one backend, because the container memory includes cache and shared buffers.

spec.title: Context switches per second (host)
spec.description: node_context_switches_total is for the whole machine, not only Postgres: compare pool sizes, do not read the absolute value. Prediction: grows with the number of busy backends sharing 2 cores. B1 probes showed about 45 to 59 k/s at small pools.

spec.title: Host disk utilization (io_time share)
spec.description: Share of time the disk had I/O in flight. B1 showed about 97% near the knee, so the shared fsync disk is the likely next limit for every pool size. Near 100% means more connections cannot help.

spec.title: Host disk write latency (await, seconds)
spec.description: write time / writes completed. B1 probes showed about 1.2 to 1.3 ms. Rising with pool size means writes queue on the disk.

spec.title: Node process CPU (cores)
spec.description: User and system CPU of ingest-api. One thread runs JS, so about 1 core is its ceiling (B1 probes: 18 to 24% of a core at 1000 to 1500 req/s). If this nears 1.0 at pool 25 and up, Node is the next limit, not Postgres.

spec.title: Event loop delay p99
spec.description: How late the JS thread runs its timers. Above about 100 ms the JS thread is blocked. Not expected to be the story in B2.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (0 expected for pool 25 and up)
spec.description: k6 could not start a request because all VUs were busy. For pool 5 and 10 dropping is part of the finding (server too slow); for pool 25 and up it must be 0, otherwise the generator or the server has a problem.

spec.title: k6 VUs vs max
spec.description: Active VUs against the cap (3000). Reaching the cap limits the longest queue wait to about 3000 / capacity, which decides whether pool_timeout can appear at all.

spec.title: Generator CPU busy (k6 CPUs, keep under 70%)
spec.description: Host CPU busy on the CPUs k6 is pinned to (3, 9, 4, 10). Above 70% the generator may be the limit and the run says nothing about the server.

spec.title: Listen queue overflows and drops
spec.description: Accept-queue trouble on the server port. Expected 0 (not the subject of B2). Non-zero means part of the failure came from the accept queue, not the pool.

spec.title: Postgres exporter up and server DB errors (all types)
spec.description: pg_up = 1 means the exporter reaches Postgres. At pool 120 Postgres may be full and the exporter itself may fail to connect (pg_up = 0): then the Postgres panels have gaps exactly where it matters. ep_db_errors_total counts all 503 caused by DB or pool errors, without the type.

spec.title: Node heap and RSS
spec.description: Queued requests live in memory: RSS grows when many requests wait (B1: 529 MB after a collapsed run). Surprising growth at pool 25 and up.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: what happened for each pool size
2. The mechanism: waiting for a connection vs the cost of connections
3. Resource view: what the connections cost
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run
